dictation: New patient visit. Forty two year old male, new to our practice, with three months of low back pain radiating down the left leg to the lateral foot. Numbness in the left lateral foot. Weakness with plantar flexion. Exam shows positive straight leg raise on the left at forty degrees, diminished left Achilles reflex, four out of five left gastrocnemius strength. I personally reviewed his outside MRI of the lumbar spine which shows a large left paracentral disc herniation at L5 S1 compressing the left S1 nerve root. Assessment: lumbar disc herniation at L5 S1 with left S1 radiculopathy. Plan: physical therapy, a medrol dose pack, and referral for a left L5 S1 transforaminal epidural steroid injection. Follow up in six weeks. Moderate complexity medical decision making.
note:
SUBJECTIVE:
42-year-old male, new to practice, presents with three months of low back pain radiating down the left leg to the lateral foot. Reports numbness in the left lateral foot and weakness with plantar flexion. No other systemic complaints documented. New patient; outside MRI reviewed.

OBJECTIVE:
- Neuro/musculoskeletal exam:
  - Positive straight leg raise on the left at 40 degrees.
  - Diminished left Achilles (S1) reflex.
  - Left gastrocnemius (plantar flexion) strength 4/5.
- Imaging:
  - Outside lumbar spine MRI reviewed: large left paracentral L5–S1 disc herniation compressing the left S1 nerve root.

ASSESSMENT:
1. Lumbar disc herniation at L5–S1 with left S1 radiculopathy — consistent with history, exam, and MRI findings.

PLAN:
- Initiate physical therapy focused on lumbar stabilization, core strengthening, and radicular symptom management.
- Start Medrol dose pack (methylprednisolone taper) for short course anti-inflammatory therapy.
- Refer for left L5–S1 transforaminal epidural steroid injection for targeted radicular pain control.
- Advise return/follow-up in 6 weeks to reassess symptoms, strength, and reflexes; sooner if worsening neurological deficits, progressive weakness, or bowel/bladder dysfunction.
- Documented moderate complexity medical decision making.

Plan: continue home exercise program, gabapentin three hundred milligrams at night, and discussed L4 L5 decompression if symptoms worsen. Moderate medical decision making. Return in three months.
note:

71-year-old female established patient with known lumbar spinal stenosis at L4–L5. - Counseling provided regarding surgical option: L4–L5 decompression if symptoms worsen or functional decline occurs.

- Return to clinic in 3 months or sooner if worsening symptoms, new neurologic deficits, or bowel/bladder changes.

dictation: New patient consultation. Sixty three year old male with progressive hand clumsiness, difficulty buttoning shirts, and gait imbalance over six months. Exam: positive Hoffmann sign bilaterally, hyperreflexia in the upper and lower extremities, wide based gait, positive Romberg. MRI of the cervical spine reviewed shows severe spinal canal stenosis at C5 C6 and C6 C7 from disc osteophyte complexes with T2 signal change in the spinal cord at C5 C6. Assessment: cervical spondylotic myelopathy at C5 C6 and C6 C7. Plan: recommend anterior cervical discectomy and fusion at C5 C6 and C6 C7. Risks benefits and alternatives discussed and the patient agrees to surgery. High complexity decision making.
note:
SUBJECTIVE:
63-year-old male new patient with a 6-month history of progressive hand clumsiness and impaired fine motor tasks (difficulty buttoning shirts) and progressive gait imbalance. No other symptoms reported in the note. Patient understands condition and agrees to recommended intervention.

OBJECTIVE:
Neurologic exam notable for bilateral positive Hoffmann sign, hyperreflexia in both upper and lower extremities, wide-based gait, and positive Romberg. Cervical spine MRI reviewed: severe spinal canal stenosis at C5–C6 and C6–C7 due to disc-osteophyte complexes with T2 intramedullary signal change at C5–C6 consistent with myelomalacia.

ASSESSMENT:
1. Cervical spondylotic myelopathy, levels C5–C6 and C6–C7, with clinical signs of myelopathy (upper motor neuron findings, gait dysfunction) and radiographic evidence of severe canal stenosis and cord signal change at C5–C6.

PLAN:
- Recommend surgical decompression: anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) at C5–C6 and C6–C7.
- Discussed risks, benefits, and alternatives (including conservative management, posterior decompression options); patient consents to proceed with surgery.
- Risk/benefit discussion documented; decision-making complexity high.
- Preoperative workup: obtain routine labs, ECG as indicated, surgical clearance, and anesthesia evaluation.
- Schedule operative planning and preop imaging/templating; counsel on postoperative expectations, activity restrictions, and follow-up.

dictation: New patient visit. Forty eight year old female with right sided neck pain radiating into the right thumb and index finger for eight weeks. Positive Spurling test on the right. Right biceps and brachioradialis reflexes diminished. Right wrist extension four out of five. MRI shows a right foraminal disc herniation at C5 C6 compressing the right C6 nerve root. Assessment: cervical disc herniation at C5 C6 with right C6 radiculopathy. Plan: physical therapy, nonsteroidal anti inflammatory medication, and a cervical epidural steroid injection. Return in six weeks.
note:
SUBJECTIVE:
48-year-old female, new patient, presents with eight weeks of right-sided neck pain radiating into the right thumb and index finger. Symptoms consistent with radicular pain in the C6 distribution. Reports no prior surgeries. No bowel or bladder symptoms documented.

OBJECTIVE:
Right-sided Spurling test positive. Right biceps and brachioradialis reflexes diminished. Right wrist extension strength 4/5. MRI cervical spine: right foraminal disc herniation at C5–C6 compressing the right C6 nerve root.

ASSESSMENT:
Cervical disc herniation at C5–C6 with right C6 radiculopathy causing radicular pain, diminished reflexes, and mild motor weakness (right wrist extension 4/5).

PLAN:
- Initiate physical therapy focusing on cervical stabilization, traction as indicated, and radiculopathy-directed exercises.
- Prescribe NSAID therapy (agent/dose per provider discretion) for pain/inflammation.
- Schedule right-sided cervical epidural steroid injection targeting C6 nerve root.
- Educate patient on activity modification, home exercises, and red-flag symptoms (worsening weakness, new numbness, bowel/bladder dysfunction); instruct to seek urgent care if these occur.
- Follow up in 6 weeks to reassess symptoms and neurologic exam; consider surgical consultation if progressive neurologic deficit or refractory pain.

dictation: Established patient. Sixty six year old female with degenerative spondylolisthesis at L4 L5, grade one, with severe central and lateral recess stenosis and bilateral L5 radiculopathy. She failed six months of physical therapy, two epidural steroid injections, and medications. Flexion extension x rays show four millimeters of motion at L4 L5. Assessment: degenerative spondylolisthesis L4 L5 with spinal stenosis and neurogenic claudication. Plan: decision made today for L4 L5 laminectomy and transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion with pedicle screw instrumentation, scheduled for tomorrow. High complexity medical decision making.
note:
SUBJECTIVE:
66-year-old established female with known degenerative spondylolisthesis at L4-5 (grade 1). Reports severe central and lateral recess stenosis with bilateral L5 radiculopathy and symptoms of neurogenic claudication. Has failed conservative management: 6 months of physical therapy, two epidural steroid injections, and medication therapy. No new complaints documented.

OBJECTIVE:
Flexion-extension lumbar radiographs: 4 mm motion at L4-5. No additional vitals, neurologic exam, or imaging details provided in the record.

ASSESSMENT:
1. Degenerative spondylolisthesis L4-5, grade 1.
2. Severe central and lateral recess spinal stenosis at L4-5.
3. Bilateral L5 radiculopathy with neurogenic claudication.
Clinical course refractory to conservative measures.

PLAN:
- Proceed with surgical intervention: L4-5 laminectomy and transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) with pedicle screw instrumentation.
- Surgery scheduled for tomorrow.
- High-complexity medical decision making documented.
- Perioperative planning as per standard: preoperative clearance, informed consent, anesthesia evaluation, perioperative antibiotics, DVT prophylaxis, and postoperative rehabilitation plan (details to be completed in preop assessment).

dictation: Operative note. Diagnosis: degenerative spondylolisthesis L4 L5 with spinal stenosis and neurogenic claudication. Procedure: L4 L5 laminectomy with bilateral foraminotomies, L4 L5 transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion with insertion of an interbody cage, posterior segmental pedicle screw instrumentation L4 to L5, posterolateral fusion, local autograft and allograft bone graft. Estimated blood loss three hundred milliliters. No complications.
note:
SUBJECTIVE:
67-year-old patient with degenerative L4-L5 spondylolisthesis presenting with spinal stenosis and neurogenic claudication. Symptoms prompting surgery included progressive leg pain and limited walking tolerance consistent with neurogenic claudication. (Operative note provided; preoperative consent and indications documented by surgical team.)

OBJECTIVE:
Operative procedure performed under general anesthesia. L4-L5 laminectomy with bilateral foraminotomies completed. L4-L5 transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion performed with placement of an interbody cage. Posterior segmental pedicle screw instrumentation placed from L4 to L5. Posterolateral fusion performed using local autograft supplemented with allograft. Estimated blood loss 300 mL. No intraoperative complications reported.

ASSESSMENT:
Primary diagnosis: Degenerative spondylolisthesis L4-L5 with associated spinal stenosis and neurogenic claudication.
Postoperative status: Stable intraoperative course; instrumentation and interbody fusion implanted as planned; hemostasis achieved.

PLAN:
- Routine postoperative monitoring in PACU; neurovascular checks and pain control.
- Continue wound care per standard spine postoperative protocol; keep incision clean and dry.
- Initiate DVT prophylaxis per institutional protocol (mechanical and pharmacologic as indicated).
- Activity: mobilize with assistance as tolerated; limitations on bending, lifting, twisting per surgeon's instructions.
- Prescribe analgesics and stool softeners as needed; prescribe antibiotics perioperative per protocol.
- Arrange postoperative follow-up in clinic in approximately 2 weeks for wound check and radiographic evaluation; obtain postoperative x-rays to confirm hardware position and alignment as per surgeon’s preference.
- Educate patient on signs of infection, increased neurological deficit, or wound drainage and to seek immediate care if they occur.

dictation: Procedure note. Left L5 S1 transforaminal epidural steroid injection under fluoroscopic guidance. Indication: left S1 radiculopathy from L5 S1 disc herniation. After sterile prep, a twenty two gauge spinal needle was advanced into the left L5 S1 foramen. Contrast confirmed epidural spread without vascular uptake. Two milliliters of dexamethasone and lidocaine were injected. The patient tolerated the procedure well.
note:
SUBJECTIVE:
Patient with left S1 radiculopathy secondary to an L5-S1 disc herniation presenting for left L5-S1 transforaminal epidural steroid injection. Symptoms consistent with radicular pain in left S1 distribution. No complications or intolerance reported by patient prior to procedure.

OBJECTIVE:
Procedure performed under fluoroscopic guidance. After sterile preparation, a 22-gauge spinal needle advanced into the left L5-S1 neural foramen. Fluoroscopic contrast injection demonstrated appropriate epidural spread without vascular uptake. A total of 2 mL of medication (dexamethasone with lidocaine) was administered. Patient tolerated procedure well with no immediate adverse events observed.

ASSESSMENT:
1. Left S1 radiculopathy due to L5-S1 disc herniation — treated with left L5-S1 transforaminal epidural steroid injection.
2. No immediate procedural complications; contrast confirmed epidural (not intravascular) placement.

PLAN:
- Post-procedure observation for appropriate recovery; discharge when stable.
- Monitor for improvement in radicular pain over subsequent days; expect possible immediate partial relief from local anesthetic and delayed anti-inflammatory effect from steroid.
- Instruct patient to report any new or worsening symptoms (increasing pain, numbness, weakness, fever, signs of infection, or allergic reaction).
- Follow-up appointment or phone call as per clinic protocol to assess response and determine need for further interventions or repeat injections.

dictation: Procedure note. Bilateral lumbar medial branch blocks at L4 L5 and L5 S1 facet joints under fluoroscopic guidance for chronic axial low back pain due to lumbar facet arthropathy and lumbar spondylosis without radiculopathy. Bupivacaine was injected at each level. Patient reported eighty percent relief during the diagnostic window.
note:
SUBJECTIVE:
Patient with chronic axial low back pain attributed to lumbar facet arthropathy and lumbar spondylosis without radiculopathy. Presented for diagnostic bilateral lumbar medial branch blocks at L4-L5 and L5-S1. Reported approximately 80% pain relief during the diagnostic window following the procedure.

OBJECTIVE:
Procedure performed under fluoroscopic guidance. Bilateral medial branch blocks at L4-L5 and L5-S1 were identified fluoroscopically. Bupivacaine was injected at each targeted level. No immediate complications observed. Patient tolerated the procedure well.

ASSESSMENT:
1. Chronic axial low back pain secondary to lumbar facet arthropathy and lumbar spondylosis without radiculopathy.
2. Diagnostic bilateral lumbar medial branch blocks at L4-L5 and L5-S1 with bupivacaine resulted in approximately 80% temporary pain relief — consistent with positive diagnostic blocks indicating facet-mediated pain.

PLAN:
- Given positive diagnostic response, discuss proceeding with bilateral radiofrequency ablation (medial branch neurotomy) of L4-L5 and L5-S1 medial branches as next therapeutic option.
- Review risks, benefits, and alternatives with patient and obtain consent if proceeding.
- Provide post-procedure instructions: activity as tolerated, monitor for increased pain, bleeding, infection, or signs of adverse reaction; acetaminophen or prescribed analgesics as needed.
- Follow-up appointment to review outcomes and plan definitive intervention (RFA) in 1–2 weeks or sooner if symptoms change.

Indication: lumbar facet joint syndrome and lumbar spondylosis without myelopathy or radiculopathy, with greater than eighty percent relief from two prior diagnostic medial branch blocks. Lesions were created at eighty degrees Celsius for ninety seconds. No complications.
note:
SUBJECTIVE:
Patient with history of lumbar facet joint syndrome and lumbar spondylosis without myelopathy or radiculopathy. Prior diagnostic medial branch blocks provided >80% pain relief. Patient presented for radiofrequency ablation for persistent facet-mediated low back pain.

OBJECTIVE:
Procedure: Right L4–L5 and L5–S1 lumbar medial branch radiofrequency ablation performed under fluoroscopic guidance. Lesions created at 80°C for 90 seconds at each targeted medial branch. No intraprocedural complications. Hemostasis adequate. Patient tolerated procedure well.

ASSESSMENT:
1. Lumbar facet joint syndrome (right L4–5 and L5–S1) — treated with therapeutic radiofrequency ablation of medial branch nerves.
2. Lumbar spondylosis without myelopathy or radiculopathy.

PLAN:
- Post-procedure observation per routine protocols; discharge when stable.
- Routine post-procedure instructions: activity as tolerated, avoid strenuous lifting for 24–48 hours, local soreness expected; use ice/acetaminophen/NSAIDs as needed unless contraindicated.
- Monitor for complications (increasing pain, fever, numbness, weakness, wound issues); return to clinic or ED if occur.
- Follow-up arranged per clinic protocol (typically 4–12 weeks) to assess pain relief and functional improvement.
- Continue other conservative measures as previously recommended (physical therapy, home exercise program, analgesics) as indicated.

dictation: Established patient. Sixty two year old female, eighteen months after L5 S1 posterior fusion, with recurrent low back pain. CT scan shows nonunion at L5 S1 with lucency around both S1 pedicle screws and a broken left S1 screw. Assessment: pseudarthrosis after lumbar fusion at L5 S1 and mechanical breakdown of the internal fixation device of the vertebrae. Plan: revision posterior fusion with removal and replacement of instrumentation. Discussed risks and benefits.
note:
SUBJECTIVE:
62-year-old female, established patient, presents 18 months status-post L5-S1 posterior fusion with recurrent low back pain. Reports persistent/recurrent lumbar pain since prior surgery. No additional history provided regarding radicular symptoms, neurologic deficits, systemic symptoms, or prior medical comorbidities in the note. Patient understands imaging findings and surgical recommendations after discussion of risks and benefits.

OBJECTIVE:
CT lumbar spine demonstrates nonunion (pseudarthrosis) at L5-S1 with lucency surrounding both S1 pedicle screws and a broken left S1 screw. No other objective exam findings documented in the provided information.

ASSESSMENT:
1. Pseudarthrosis (nonunion) at L5-S1 following prior posterior lumbar fusion.
2. Mechanical failure of posterior instrumentation: lucency around bilateral S1 pedicle screws and fractured left S1 pedicle screw.
3. Recurrent low back pain likely secondary to hardware failure and pseudarthrosis.

PLAN:
- Recommend revision posterior fusion at L5-S1 with removal of existing instrumentation and replacement of hardware.
- Discussed risks, benefits, and alternatives of revision surgery with the patient.
- Preoperative planning: obtain routine pre-op clearance, recent labs, and any necessary imaging (full lumbar radiographs and consideration of CT for planning if not recent).
- Plan for intraoperative removal of broken screw, debridement of pseudarthrosis, possible extension of fusion levels as indicated, and placement of new instrumentation with augmentation/grafting as needed (autograft/allograft/biologics to promote fusion).
- Arrange surgical scheduling, preoperative consultation, and consent. Follow-up for pre-op clearance and perioperative instructions.

dictation: New patient. Twenty nine year old male who fell from a ladder at work six days ago and sustained a stable burst fracture of the L1 vertebral body, initial encounter. Neurologically intact. No retropulsion causing canal compromise. Plan: thoracolumbosacral orthosis brace, upright x rays in two weeks, pain control. This is a workers compensation injury.
note:
SUBJECTIVE:
29-year-old male, new patient, presents for evaluation following a fall from a ladder at work six days ago. Reports acute back pain since the injury localized to the lower thoracic/upper lumbar region. Denies numbness, tingling, weakness, bowel or bladder dysfunction. Injury is work-related and will be managed as worker's compensation.

OBJECTIVE:
Neurologic exam: intact motor strength and sensation in bilateral lower extremities; no focal deficits noted. No signs of spinal cord compression. Imaging (prior): L1 burst fracture described as stable with no retropulsion causing canal compromise. (Plan for upright x-rays in two weeks to reassess alignment.)

ASSESSMENT:
1. Stable burst fracture of L1 vertebral body — initial encounter.
2. No neurologic deficit; no canal compromise on prior imaging.
3. Occupational (worker's compensation) injury.

PLAN:
- Conservative management with thoracolumbosacral orthosis (TLSO) brace; patient to wear as instructed.
- Pain control: prescribe/advise appropriate analgesics (NSAID and/or short course opioid as needed) and consider muscle relaxant if indicated. (Prescriptions per clinic protocol — arrange as needed.)
- Activity: limited/modified duty per brace and work restrictions; avoid heavy lifting, bending, twisting until reassessment.
- Imaging: obtain upright lumbar spine x-rays in 2 weeks to evaluate alignment and stability.
- Follow-up: clinic follow-up after x-rays or sooner if worsening pain, new neurologic symptoms, or other concerns.
- Document as worker's compensation; provide necessary paperwork for employer/claims.

dictation: New patient. Sixty seven year old female with a history of breast cancer treated five years ago, now with new mid back pain. MRI shows a lesion in the T10 vertebral body with pathologic compression fracture, consistent with metastatic disease to bone. No spinal cord compression. Assessment: secondary malignant neoplasm of bone, T10 pathologic fracture. Plan: CT guided biopsy, oncology referral, radiation oncology consult, and bracing.
note:
SUBJECTIVE:
67-year-old female, new patient. History of breast cancer treated five years ago. Presents with new mid-back pain. No reported neurological deficits or symptoms of spinal cord compression noted in the provided history.

OBJECTIVE:
MRI: Lesion in the T10 vertebral body with pathologic compression fracture. No evidence of spinal cord compression on imaging. No additional physical exam findings provided.

ASSESSMENT:
1. Secondary malignant neoplasm of bone — lesion involving T10 vertebral body, suspicious for metastatic breast cancer.
2. Pathologic compression fracture of T10.
3. No spinal cord compression identified on MRI.

PLAN:
- CT-guided biopsy of the T10 lesion to obtain tissue diagnosis.
- Referral to medical oncology for systemic management given concern for metastatic breast cancer.
- Referral to radiation oncology for consideration of palliative/spinal radiation to T10.
- Spinal bracing for stabilization and pain management as indicated.
- Pain control as needed (coordinate analgesics with oncology/pain management).
- Obtain baseline labs and consider staging scans per oncology recommendations (e.g., CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, bone scan or PET-CT) after biopsy results.
- Close follow-up after biopsy and specialist evaluations; urgent re-evaluation if new neurologic symptoms (weakness, numbness, bowel/bladder changes) develop.

dictation: Established patient. Thirty nine year old office worker with mechanical low back pain and neck pain for one month. No radiating pain, no numbness, no weakness. Exam: normal neurologic exam, mild paraspinal muscle spasm. Assessment: low back pain and cervicalgia, muscle spasm of back. Plan: ergonomic changes, physical therapy, ibuprofen. Low complexity.
medicalPractice: Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation (Physiatry) / Primary Care — Musculoskeletal
note:
SUBJECTIVE:
39-year-old established patient, office worker, presents with one month of mechanical low back pain and neck pain. No radicular symptoms: denies radiating pain, numbness, or weakness. Symptoms consistent with activity/posture-related pain.

OBJECTIVE:
Physical exam: normal neurologic exam (no sensory deficit, no motor weakness, reflexes intact). Mild paraspinal muscle spasm noted in cervical and lumbar regions. No signs of acute neurocompression.

ASSESSMENT:
1. Mechanical low back pain.
2. Cervicalgia (neck pain).
3. Paraspinal muscle spasm.

PLAN:
- Education on ergonomic changes at work (adjust chair, monitor height, lumbar support, frequent position changes/mini-breaks).
- Prescribe/refer for physical therapy focusing on posture correction, core and cervical strengthening, stretching, and manual therapy as indicated.
- Recommend ibuprofen (e.g., 400 mg PO every 6–8 hours as needed with food), barring contraindications; advise maximum daily dose and to consult if on other anticoagulants/NSAIDs or history of GI/renal disease.
- Encourage home exercises and application of heat/ice as tolerated.
- Return precautions: worsening pain, development of radicular symptoms, numbness, weakness, bowel/bladder changes — seek earlier evaluation.
- Follow-up in 4–6 weeks to assess response or sooner if symptoms progress. Low-complexity visit.
